```{=html}
<div id="a14-explain" class="lx-xgrid">

<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Value of lost load</dt><dd>What an hour or a kWh without power costs someone; it differs by customer and by outage length.</dd><dt>Expected outage cost</dt><dd>Outages a year × their length × the cost of an hour, summed over outage lengths: $70,200 a year for the hospital here.</dd><dt>The next hour</dt><dd>Buy another hour of backup while it saves more a year than it costs; then check that the whole design covers its fixed costs.</dd><dt>Value stacking</dt><dd>Everyday savings can carry a design that outage savings alone cannot.</dd><dt>Who owns it</dt><dd>The net is the same for everyone together; the owner decides who pays, who gains and who carries the risk.</dd></dl><table class="lx-mini-table a14-tab"><caption class="lx-hint">Four owners of the battery-and-generator design (illustrative deals and rates)</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Owner</th><th scope="col">Who pays</th><th scope="col">Carries the risk</th><th scope="col">Annual cost</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>The utility (7%)</td><td>All the utility's customers, through rates its state regulator approves</td><td>The customers, if the regulator lets the cost into rates; the utility's shareholders, if not</td><td class="n">$104,476</td></tr><tr><td>A rural co-op (5%)</td><td>The co-op's members, through their rates</td><td>The members: the co-op borrows, and has no shares to sell</td><td class="n">$94,521</td></tr><tr><td>The county (4%)</td><td>County taxpayers, from its budget</td><td>The taxpayers</td><td class="n">$89,784</td></tr><tr><td>A private company (10%)</td><td>The campus: a fixed yearly fee in a long contract</td><td>The company carries cost overruns and breakdowns; the campus pays the fee even in calm years</td><td class="n">$120,518</td></tr></tbody></table>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Spreading a cost over the years</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A sum paid now becomes a cost a year through the [capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}, CRF:

$$\text{CRF} = \frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}$$

- $r$ is the borrowing rate a year (here 7%, or the owner's) and $n$ the number of years (15). At 7% over 15 years, CRF ≈ 0.1098: $740,000 of equipment costs about $81,248 a year.
- [K3](k03-discounting.html) explains discounting; Analyst lesson A1 (upcoming) builds a project's cash flows year by year.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Letting a solver choose the sizes</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- This lesson tests one size at a time. A sizing model chooses battery, generator and solar together, hour by hour, and can treat the hospital's survival as a rule rather than a cost.
- A rule ("survive 72 hours") and a cost ("an hour without power costs $9,000") can give different designs: the second weighs the rare long outages by how rarely they come.
- Modeler lesson M5 (upcoming) sizes a microgrid that must survive an outage.

## Check yourself, then practise
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Three myths and one question, then a practice set of about 30 minutes.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a14-myth">
<!-- a14-myth:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="pays" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A microgrid that keeps a hospital open always pays for itself.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here a 2-hour battery comes out at −$48,849 a year on outages alone, and at +$5,151 with its everyday savings.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="voll" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The value of lost load is one number.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the 2025 co-op survey, an 8-hour outage cost a household $3.22 and a business $41 per kWh not delivered.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="owner" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If a microgrid saves money overall, its owner comes out ahead.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The owner pays the capital and gains only through rates, a fee or the savings it keeps. Its borrowing rate moves the total too: +$3,682 a year for everyone together at 10%, +$34,416 at 4%.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- a14-myth:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a14">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="expected" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Outages of 4 hours hit the campus 0.4 times a year, and the hospital loses $9,000 an hour. What do they cost the hospital in a year, on average?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$3,600</li><li data-value="b">$14,400</li><li data-value="c">$36,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$14,400: 0.4 outages × 4 hours × $9,000 an hour.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="a14-practice" class="lx-card">
<!-- a14-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><p class="lx-hint">Use the numbers in the steps above (2025 dollars; the campus's are illustrative).</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>Expected outage hours.</b> Outages of 1, 4, 12, 36 and 72 hours happen 0.8, 0.4, 0.15, 0.06 and 0.02 times a year. How many hours without power a year, on average?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7.8 hours: 0.8 × 1 + 0.4 × 4 + 0.15 × 12 + 0.06 × 36 + 0.02 × 72.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The fifth hour of battery.</b> At $9,000 an hour, what does a battery's fifth hour save a year? Does it pay at $14,975?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Outages longer than 4 hours happen 0.23 times a year, so it saves $2,070 a year: far below $14,975.</p></details></li><li><p><b>When the first hour passes.</b> At what cost of an hour without power would the battery's first hour save as much as it costs?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$14,975 ÷ 1.43 outages a year = $10,472 an hour. The fixed costs would still need covering.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Value against price.</b> A household's 24-hour outage costs $1.96 per kWh not delivered. How many times the 17.23¢ it pays per kWh?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 11 times.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The cost of borrowing.</b> The battery-and-generator design costs $740,000 to build, spread over 15 years. Its capital cost a year at 4% and at 10%?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$66,556 and $97,291: the same equipment, $30,734 a year apart.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The mill's hours.</b> Why does the mill at midday lower the village's cost per kWh, while the mill in the evening helps less?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>At midday the panels run the mill directly: $0.31 falls to $0.23. In the evening the battery must grow from 40 to 70 kWh: $0.28.</p></details></li></ol>
<!-- a14-practice:end -->
</div>
```

```{=html}
<li>FERC (2023). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2024-01/24_Energy-Markets-Primer_0117_DIGITAL_0.pdf">2024 Energy Primer: A Handbook of Energy Market Basics</a> (PDF), pp. 35, 36 and 130. December 2023.</li>
<li>U.S. DOE and NREL (2019). <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2019/12/f69/01_microgrids-Woods.pdf">Microgrids</a> (PDF), slides 4 and 6: what microgrids are built for, and why their resilience is hard to value. 11 December 2019.</li>
<li>Li et al. (2023). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Facility and microgrid location-allocation for integrated supply chain and transactive energy operations</a>. Applied Mathematical Modelling 119, 119–136.</li>
```
